sources.quote: Stalls selling Tibetan jewelry and souveniers line the Barkhor. Prayer wheels, coral, turquoise and silver jewelry and Tibetan Buddhist trumpets, pictured here, are favorites.
is the commercial center and busiest street of the old city of Lhasa, Tibet.

facts.rationale: Resolved supported. NPR (2006, T2, quote verified on page) says stalls selling jewellery, prayer wheels and souvenirs line the Barkhor; Wikipedia calls it Lhasa's commercial centre. Lonely Planet notes the souvenir stalls were later moved into the Barkhor Supermarket building, so 'stalls' is somewhat dated, but shops still line the circuit.

sources.quote: These layers of city quarters are entered by crooked little alleyways, lined by low, white-washed stone-and-mud houses.
The Barkhor is an area of narrow streets and a public square in the old part of the city located around Jokhang Temple

facts.rationale: Resolved supported. The Tibet Heritage Fund report on asianart.com (quote verified) describes the old-city quarters as crooked alleyways lined by white-washed houses; Wikipedia Architecture of Lhasa confirms narrow streets. B found the narrow lanes but missed the whitewash source.

sources.quote: The circumference of Barkhor Street is about 1,000 meters, originated in the 7th century A.D.
Barkhor is the oldest street in Lhasa

facts.rationale: Wikipedia: originated 7th century, oldest street (THF dates the present Barkor to at least the late 14th c.).

sources.quote: The oldest part of the temple was built in 652 by Songtsen Gampo.

facts.rationale: Jokhang built 652 by Songtsen Gampo.

sources.quote: The intermediate circle, the Barkor, has existed at least since the late 14th century
The innermost pilgrimage circle, the Nangkor, which leads around the Tsuglakhang's central temple building

facts.rationale: Resolved supported. Tibet Heritage Fund report (asianart.com, quote verified) calls the Barkor the intermediate circle between the Nangkor and the outer route; no T1 source contradicts the 'middle circuit' reading.

sources.quote: The white-washed facade is further accentuated by thick black frames around and little slate roofs above the doors and windows.
The dark band of red at the top, dotted with white paint, was, in previous eras, a mark reserved for certain noble houses.

facts.rationale: Resolved supported. THF report (asianart.com, verified) gives the white-washed facade with thick black frames; the asianart kora photo essay records red bands on Barkhor-kora houses (noble houses). 'Many' with red trim is loose but not contradicted.

sources.quote: first built the Jokhang, where Tibetan Buddhism believers began to turn around the monastery, and gradually formed a road

facts.rationale: Development tied to the 7th-century Jokhang.

sources.quote: is the commercial center and busiest street of the old city of Lhasa, Tibet.
Today, as it has been for centuries, the Barkor is also Lhasa's main bazaar street.

facts.rationale: Commercial centre / main bazaar street.

sources.quote: the outer pilgrim road in Lhasa matching its inner twin, Barkhor.
The Barkhor is a popular devotional circumambulation around the historic Jokhang for pilgrims and locals.

facts.rationale: Resolved supported. Wikipedia Lhasa (T1, quote verified) calls the Barkhor the inner twin of the Lingkhor; the THF report's 'intermediate circle' (A's source) counts the Nangkor inside the temple, a different frame, and a T2 framing cannot override the T1 wording. Not false.
